newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian Broadcasting Corp Morning Update.

text.p: TWO FAILED ATTEMPTS TO FREE PILOT LED TO DEATHS
Two unsuccessful attempts to free Australian pilot Justin Fraser from a prison in Somalia resulted in the death of several people.
The revelation follows the release of Mr Fraser, who's now resting in Nairobi after spending four months in detention.
The young pilot was set free from his prison cell in Baidoa, following a direct appeal from the Kenyan President, Daniel arap Moi.
Australian diplomats were unaware of Mr Fraser's release until he'd arrived in Nairobi.
Australia's High Commissioner to Kenya, John Trotter, says during his captivity, Somali militamen made two failed attempts to rescue Mr Fraser, leaving a number of people dead.
TAX REFORM SUMMIT UNDERWAY TODAY
The National tax reform summit, which gets underway in Canberra today, has been declared a politician free zone, to give community and business groups a chance to contribute to the taxation debate.
The event is a joint effort of the Australian Council of Social Service and the Chamber of Commerce and Industry.
The summit comes after a week of renewed debate over the merits of taxation reform.
Victorian Premier Jeff Kennett wants a goods and services tax introduced, while Deputy Federal Labor Leader Gareth Evans has argued the case for overall revenue increases.
BRYANT HAS NEW LAWYER
The alleged Port Arthur gunman, Martin Bryant, will be represented by his new lawyer in a short mention hearing in the Criminal Court in Hobart this morning.
Hobart barrister, John Avery, has taken up the defence brief, after Mr Bryant's original lawyer, David Gunson, announced earlier this week that he was no longer representing him.
Mr Avery says he had a cordial meeting with Mr Bryant at Risdon prison yesterday, and is confident the trial, set to begin on the 19th of November, will not be delayed.
On Monday, Martin Bryant pleaded not guilty in the Supreme Court, to 72 charges, including 35 of murder, relating to the Port Arthur shootings in April.
TNT DOCUMENTS TO BE LOOKED AT
The Australian Securities Commission will meet with Stock Exchange officals today to look at the documentation associated with the TNT takeover.
Irregular volumes of options transactions were detected ahead of the announcement this week of a two-billion dollar takeover of TNT by the Dutch postal and telecommunications company, KPN.

The ASC's Irene O'Brien says they're not sure whether there's been a breach of the coporations law, or if market forces have combined to cause a glitch on the Stock Exchange's computer surveillance equipment.
SUPER LEAGUE RULING TODAY
The Australian Rugby League chairman, Ken Arthurson, says he hopes breakaway clubs will just get on with the game if Super League loses its appeal today.
The Federal Court is due to hand down its verdict in Sydney this afternoon on News Limited's appeal against the court ban on Super League until at least the year 2000.
Mr Arthurson says he doesn't know how some of the clubs that have been disloyal to the ARL and have helped plot its downfall will feel about being part of the fold again.
But he doesn't think there'll be a spoiling process by New Limited if the appeal fails.
Both the ARL and News Limited camps are optimistic about today's verdict.
Media baron Rupert Murdoch returns to Australia today, having invested more than A$125 million in the Super League concept in this country.
MORE CYCLONES TO HIT TOP END
The Top End's being warned it may be in for more cyclones this wet season.
The weather bureau in Darwin says the passing of the El Nino effect could mean the Territory will experience more cyclone activity than normal.
Senior Forecaster Jeff Dool says extensive scientific research has been carried out including an assessment of the sea surface temperatures to the North.
HERRON BRACES FOR CONTROVERSY
Federal Aboriginal Affairs Minister, John Herron, says there will be controversey when he announces the number of Aboriginal groups which will no longer be funded.
The announcement will follow a special audit of ATSIC.
Newspaper reports have claimed a preliminary audit has identified rorts worth twenty-seven million-dollars by 66 aboriginal groups out of 1,300 scrutinised.
John Herron says he won't know how many groups will have their funds cut off, until the final audit is released in the next two weeks.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
